Left: comparing degrees only, every node has degree 2 (badges), so could_be_isomorphic(h, properties=d) returns True. Right: the default properties also count triangles per node, 0 on the cycle and 1 on every triangle node (badges in the accent color), so could_be_isomorphic(h) returns False and the graphs are certainly not isomorphic." width="100%"} Isomorphic graphs must agree on every structural property of their nodes. This method compares a few such properties, node by node, and returns `False` as soon as the two graphs differ, which proves they are not isomorphic. A `True` result only means that no difference was found; use `is_isomorphic()` for a definite answer. It is a cheap first filter when comparing many graphs. The properties, selected by letters in `properties=`, are: - `"d"`: degree (in- and out-degree on directed graphs) - `"t"`: number of triangles through the node (undirected graphs only) - `"c"`: number of maximal cliques containing the node (undirected graphs only) The graphs pass when the sorted lists of per-node property tuples are equal, and when they have the same directedness, number of nodes and number of edges. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The `Graph` to compare with. [properties]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["dtc"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Which properties to compare, as a string of the letters above. Default `"dtc"`. Triangle and clique counts are skipped on directed graphs. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `False` if the graphs certainly are not isomorphic, `True` if they might be. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `properties=` contains a letter other than `d`, `t` or `c`. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Degrees cost $O(V + E)$, triangle counts $O(E^{3/2})$ and maximal cliques are enumerated with Bron-Kerbosch, which is exponential in the worst case but fast on sparse graphs. NetworkX's `could_be_isomorphic` compares the same three properties, except that it does not check node and edge counts first. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A six-node cycle and two triangles have the same degrees, but each triangle node lies on a triangle, so the triangle counts tell them apart: ::: {#8edad4e1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec hexagon = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(6) two_triangles = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(3).add_cycle_graph(3) hexagon.could_be_isomorphic(two_triangles, properties="d"), hexagon.could_be_isomorphic( two_triangles ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: ::: Passing is not proof. The 4 x 4 rook's graph and the Shrikhande graph agree on degrees and triangle counts (every node has degree 6 and lies on 6 triangles), so they pass with `properties="dt"`, yet they are not isomorphic: their maximal cliques differ (the rook's graph is built from 4-cliques, the Shrikhande graph only has triangles), which `"c"` detects, and `is_isomorphic()` confirms.
